engine.title: Multibagger ideas refresh weekly, not daily
engine.body: The five names on the multibagger ticker come from the newest row of the Saturday scan and hold until the next Saturday. The prices beside them are live and tick all week, which made a fixed list of names read as a stalled feed. The scan is running on schedule; the cadence was simply never stated anywhere a reader could see it.
engine.note: The segment is labelled WEEKLY on the rail now, and the ticker query already drops the whole segment if the newest scan is more than 31 days old — so a scan that genuinely stops disappears rather than quietly serving month-old ideas as current.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Endgame: Pawn Endgames
chess.body: If you're a pawn up in a king+pawn endgame, you usually win. Key concepts: 1. Opposition — control the square in front of your pawn. 2. The square of the pawn — if the opposing king can't enter the square, your pawn promotes. 3. Key squares — a pawn on e4's key squares are d6, e6, f6. Reach them with your king and you win.

wisdom.title: Being Present
wisdom.body: Your daughter doesn't need a perfect father. She needs a present one. Put the phone down for 20 minutes when you get home. Look her in the eyes. Play on the floor. These moments are the whole point. Work can wait. She is growing every day whether you show up or not.

book.author: Morgan Housel
book.chapter: You Are Not a Spreadsheet. You Are a Person with Emotions.
book.lesson: The financial advice that is mathematically optimal is often behaviourally impossible. A 100% equity portfolio maximises long-run returns — but if you panic and sell at the bottom of every crash, you'd have been better off in a balanced fund. Housel's argument: the best investment strategy is the one you can actually stick to. Reasonable > rational. A plan that accounts for human psychology beats a theoretically perfect plan that you'll abandon when the market drops 40%. Know your emotional tolerances. Build them into your plan.
book.key_quote: The highest return is earned by the investor who can survive the worst years, not the one with the best spreadsheet.
book.action: Ask yourself: if my portfolio dropped 40% tomorrow, what would I do? Build a strategy you'd actually execute in that scenario.
crux: Doing well with money has little to do with intelligence and everything to do with behaviour.
No one is crazy. Every money decision makes sense given that person's specific history of experience.
Luck and risk are the shadow siblings of every outcome. Neither is measurable, both are decisive.
There is no reason to risk what you have for what you don't need.
Compounding is counterintuitive: $81.5bn of Buffett's $84.5bn arrived after his 65th birthday.
Getting money and keeping money are different skills. The second requires frugality and paranoia.
Tails drive everything. A minority of events account for the majority of outcomes.
The highest dividend money pays is control over your own time.
Wealth is what you don't see. Spending is evidence of spending, not of wealth.
Save without a specific goal. Savings buy optionality against a world you cannot forecast.
Room for error is the single most underrated force. Plan for the plan not going to plan.
Avoid extreme financial commitments — your future self's goals will not match your current ones.
Volatility is the fee for high returns, not a fine for a mistake. Fees you pay willingly; fines you avoid.
Define the game you are playing, and stop taking cues from people playing a different one.
learnings: A mediocre strategy held for 30 years beats a brilliant one abandoned in year 3.
Most financial mistakes are emotional, so most financial fixes must be behavioural.
Survival is the prerequisite for compounding. Everything else is secondary.
Your risk tolerance is not a number. It is what you actually do at a 40% drawdown.
examples: Ronald Read, a petrol-station attendant, left $8m by buying blue chips for decades. Richard Fuscone, Harvard MBA and Merrill executive, went bankrupt in 2008.
Bill Gates went to one of the only high schools on earth with a computer in 1968 — one in a million odds. His equally able friend Kent Evans died climbing.
Buffett's returns are good but not historically unique; his 80-year runway is. Start at 30 instead of 10 and the fortune largely disappears.
adapt: SIP ₹5–15K/month for the BMW fund. The consistency matters more than the monthly amount.
Keep 6 months of KL expenses liquid before scaling any trading capital. Room for error first.
Trading capital is separate from family capital. Never one pool.
The Dubai target is AED 30K/month, not 'as much as possible'. Define enough or the goalpost moves forever.

minimalism.title: One In, One Out
minimalism.body: Nothing enters the house until something leaves it. Not a rule about tidiness — a rule about equilibrium. Without it, possessions only ever accumulate, because buying is a decision and discarding never is.
minimalism.action: Buy nothing today without naming what it replaces.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Punctuality Is A Statement About Whose Time Matters
etiquette.body: Being late says your time is worth more than theirs, whatever you intended. Arrive five minutes early and use the wait. Note that Gulf meetings may start late — you still arrive on time.
etiquette.action: Add 10 minutes of buffer to every appointment this week.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: The Evening Shutdown
stillness.body: A defined end to the workday — review tomorrow's three priorities, close the laptop, say a phrase that marks the boundary. Without a ritual end, work bleeds into every remaining hour.
stillness.action: Pick a shutdown phrase. Use it tonight.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Map Is Not The Territory
model.body: The model is a simplification and will be wrong at the edges. A financial model is a map. Treating its outputs as facts is how forecasts become fiction.
model.action: Name the assumption in your current model most likely to be wrong.
model.label: Mental Model

drill.title: The Pre-Mortem
drill.body: Imagine the project failed. Write why. Doing this before starting surfaces risks that no optimistic planning session will ever reach.
drill.action: Pre-mortem your current priority. List three causes of death.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Muscle Is A Glucose Sink
health.body: Skeletal muscle disposes of most post-meal glucose. More muscle means better glycaemic control independent of diet — the metabolic argument for lifting, separate from strength.
health.action: A short walk or 20 bodyweight squats after your largest meal.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Kevin Systrom
quote.quote: Do what you love and the money will follow is bad advice. Do what creates the most value.

lesson.lesson: The two most important days in your life are the day you were born and the day you find out why.

case.title: Canva: Design for the Masses
case.story: Melanie Perkins was rejected by 100 VCs. Then she raised $3M. Canva now has 170M users and a $40B valuation. Key: removed complexity that designers love but others hate.
case.lesson: Simplify what experts have made complex. The mass market doesn't want power — they want results. Dumb down the interface without dumbing down the output.

fpna.title: Cost Centre vs Profit Centre
fpna.body: Cost centres are budgeted, profit centres are managed to a P&L. Knowing the difference changes how you frame every problem.

cfo.title: CFO Step 2: Investor Relations
cfo.body: Listed company CFOs speak to markets quarterly. Practice presenting results: 'Revenue grew 18% YoY driven by X. EBITDA margin expanded 200bps due to Y. FY26 guidance: Z.' Short, precise, numbers-first. Record yourself.

money_hack.title: Term Insurance First
money_hack.body: ₹1Cr term insurance (₹10–15K/year at 25). Non-negotiable. Buy this before any investment.

dubai.title: The offer letter clauses to read twice
dubai.body: Probation length (usually six months, terminable on 14 days), annual leave (30 calendar days is standard, 22 working days is not the same thing), flight allowance, and whether the visa is sponsored for family from day one or after probation.
dubai.targets: Family sponsorship after probation means six months of separation nobody mentioned.
dubai.action: Ask about family visa timing before you accept, in writing.

desk.productivity: Time-block your calendar. Unblocked time = wasted time.

father.title: Notice what she is not doing
father.do: Once a week, check the milestone list rather than assuming.
father.why: Sitting, transferring objects hand to hand, responding to her name, and babbling with consonants are the seven-month markers. Knowing the list means concerns get raised early, when intervention works best.

father.title: Talk to her about your day
father.do: Tell her what happened at work, in full sentences, as if she understands.
father.why: The content is irrelevant and the exposure is not. It also forces you to articulate the day, which is a decent end-of-work ritual in its own right.

life_wisdom.teaching: A periodic practice of reviewing one's conduct, acknowledging where one fell short, and resolving to correct it. Structurally, an audit.
life_wisdom.apply: You already run a monthly close on the business. Run a fifteen-minute one on yourself: what did I get wrong, what am I changing, what is the date.

life_wisdom.teaching: The third sublime state: genuine pleasure at another's success. Named separately because it is rarer and harder than compassion for suffering.
life_wisdom.apply: Pick the peer whose progress you find least comfortable and find the thing they did well. Envy is the most common emotion in a competitive finance function and the least admitted.

vocab.meaning: To cause something to happen suddenly.
vocab.example: The covenant test precipitated the refinancing.
vocab.note: As a verb it means trigger; as an adjective (pri-SIP-i-tit) it means hasty. Different stress.
More precise than 'stop' when something is ruled out in advance.

speaking.title: Slow the Q&A
speaking.drill: Have someone ask you three questions in a row. Pause two seconds before each answer.
speaking.why: Rapid answers read as reflexive. A deliberate pause reads as considered, and buys you the sentence you actually want.

interview_tech.q: What is the difference between EBITDA and free cash flow, and which do you manage to?
interview_tech.a: EBITDA ignores working capital movements, capex, tax and interest. A retailer can grow EBITDA while burning cash by stuffing stores with inventory and opening capital-hungry sites. Free cash flow = EBITDA − capex − change in working capital − tax − interest. Manage the business to free cash flow; report EBITDA because that is what lenders and multiples use. Where they diverge for more than two quarters, something structural is wrong.

interview_tech.q: What breaks first when a retailer scales from 60 to 200 stores?
interview_tech.a: Not the finance system — the master data and the operating cadence. Specifically: SKU and price master governance, because inconsistent data makes every report wrong; the supply chain's ability to replenish without central stock-outs; and the management reporting rhythm, because a weekly review that works for 60 stores becomes noise at 200 without exception-based reporting. Finance's job is to install store-level P&L discipline and exception thresholds before the growth, not after.

interview_soft.q: How do you decide what to delegate?
interview_soft.a: Give a rule. Something like: delegate anything where the cost of a mistake is recoverable and the learning value is high; keep anything where your specific judgement is the reason the answer is right, and anything you would have to redo. The failure mode interviewers probe is the controller who keeps the technical work because it is comfortable and delegates only the admin — which caps the team's growth and yours.

interview_soft.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your CEO.
interview_soft.a: They are testing whether you have spine and judgement, not whether you win. Use STAR and pick a disagreement where you were partly wrong — it reads as honest. Cover: what the disagreement was, what evidence you brought, how you escalated it appropriately, what the decision was, and crucially what you did after the decision went against you. The signal they want: you argue hard privately and commit fully publicly.
